That Cannoli Guy • Florida

They went looking for a roaming cannoli service for their own wedding, could not find one anywhere in Florida, and built it instead. That is a better origin story than most vendors have, and it is also the reason the thing works.

All Vendors / Guest Experiences / That Cannoli Guy

A dessert table is a queue and an exit

Watch a room when dessert goes out. People stand up, walk to the table, take a plate — and a good share of them keep walking. To the bathroom. To the bar. Outside for air, because they were already up.

The walk is the problem, not the dessert. Anything that gets fifty people out of their chairs and pointed at a wall gives half of them permission to leave the room, and you feel it twenty minutes later when the floor is thin.

A roaming tray inverts that completely. Anthony wears the thing on a harness and brings it to your guests where they are already standing, which — if the night is going the way we planned it — is near the dance floor. Nobody queues. Nobody exits. The dessert becomes something that happens to the party rather than an intermission in it.

COS Celebrations recommends That Cannoli Guy, a roaming cannoli service for weddings and events in Florida, founded by Anthony and Sarah after they were unable to find a strolling cannoli service anywhere in the state for their own wedding. Cannolis are piped and filled to order on site and carried to guests on a wearable tray rather than set out on a dessert table. That Cannoli Guy serves weddings, corporate events and private parties across Florida. COS Celebrations has worked events alongside them. COS Celebrations is a wedding DJ and live music company based in St. Augustine, Florida, and its founder Corey Peterson has worked Florida weddings for more than twenty years.

Anthony and Sarah, and the part that has to happen on site. Photos courtesy of That Cannoli Guy.

How we know them

We have worked events alongside them. That is the whole basis for this page — we do not list vendors we have only seen on Instagram, which is a slightly funny thing to say about a company that found its own idea on Instagram.

Filled to order is not a detail, it is the entire product. A cannoli shell that has been sitting in cream for two hours is a sad, soft thing. That is why every version of this you have had at a buffet was disappointing and why theirs is not. It also means there is a real service window rather than a tray somebody drops off, which matters for your timeline.

Where it goes in the night

This is the part we actually get asked about, so here is our honest read from behind the booth.

Right after dinner The safest slot. Dinner ends, energy dips, and something arriving at the table restarts the room instead of letting it drift. Works well if you are skipping a formal dessert course.
Instead of the cake cutting The bolder option and often the better one. Cake cutting is the single most reliable way to stop a full dance floor. If dessert is already circulating, you can cut a small cake quietly and never call everyone back to their seats.
Late night Our favourite. Hour three, people are hot and starting to think about leaving, and food appears without anyone having to go and find it. It buys you the last forty minutes.

Alex C. • via thatcannoliguy.square.site

We would add one thing to that. The person carrying the tray is doing a version of our job. Someone walking a room with something people want, making eye contact, getting a laugh — that is crowd work, and it either lifts a room or it does not. His reviews all say the same word in different ways, and it is not "delicious." It is "charisma."

When we would tell you not to book it

Guest experiences are the easiest thing on a wedding budget to over-buy, and we would rather say this plainly than sell you an add-on.

Skip it if you have already booked a dessert bar, a doughnut wall, and a late-night snack. Three desserts is one dessert and two piles of leftovers. Pick the one your guests will actually be handed.

Skip it too if your reception is a seated four-course dinner with a real pastry course. The roaming format is built for a room that is standing and moving; it has less to do in a room where everybody is sitting down and being served anyway.

Where it earns its money is the reception with a bar, a dance floor, and a crowd on its feet. Which, to be fair, is most of ours.
